This document is a worked example of the methods in the paper, implemented
in the **DAST** R package. It follows one analysis from raw downloads to
interpreted maps, with the checks we recommend at each step. It can function as a template that can be adapted to
other data.

# Overview

## What DAST does

DAST estimates a continuous risk surface from counts reported for areas
(polygons) when the areas change over time. For period $i$ and area $j$ the
observed count is modelled as

$$Y_{ij} \sim \text{NegBin}\Big(\textstyle\sum_{\ell} \mathcal{O}_{ij\ell}\,
\exp\{\beta_i + u(q_\ell)\},\ \tau\Big),$$

where $\mathcal{O}_{ij\ell}$ is the population (offset) of grid cell $\ell$
lying inside area $j$, $\beta_i$ is a period-specific intercept, $u(s)$ is a
Gaussian random field shared across periods, and $\tau$ is the overdispersion
parameter. Because the model works at the level of grid cells, each period
can have its own set of polygons: 2008--09 counts on one geography and
2010--12 counts on another inform the same surface $u(s)$, and no counts
need to be re-allocated between boundary sets beforehand.

## The example

We estimate under-5 mortality risk in Greater Manchester (the ten
metropolitan boroughs, E08000001--E08000010) for mid-years 2008--2012, using
death counts by Lower Layer Super Output Area (LSOA) from the Office for
National Statistics (ONS) and under-5 population from WorldPop. LSOA
boundaries were revised after the 2011 Census, so counts for 2008--09 were
originally published on 2001 LSOAs and counts for 2010 onwards on 2011 LSOAs.

```{r packages}
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(mapmisc)
library(DAST)    # install.packages("DAST")
library(aghq)
library(ggplot2)

# Use GEOS rather than s2 for polygon operations (see Section 9.4).
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
```

# Data sources, download, and freezing

| Input | Source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Deaths by LSOA, mid-year 2001--2019 | ONS ad hoc release 12626 | 5-year age bands; *all years on 2011 LSOAs* |
| LSOA 2001 and 2011 boundaries | ONS Open Geography Portal | generalised, clipped (BGC) |
| LSOA 2001 to LSOA 2011 lookup | ONS Open Geography Portal | includes change indicator `CHGIND` |
| Population by age and sex, 100 m | WorldPop Global 2000--2020 | age bands 0 (<1) and 1 (1--4) |

```{r config}
years    <- 2008:2012
gm_lads  <- sprintf("E080000%02d", 1:10)  # Greater Manchester boroughs
uk_grid  <- "EPSG:27700"                  # British National Grid, metres
data_dir <- file.path("data", "manchester")
dir.create(data_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

url_deaths <- paste0(
  "https://www.ons.gov.uk/file?uri=/peoplepopulationandcommunity/",
  "birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/adhocs/",
  "12626deathsbylowerlayersuperoutputarealsoaenglandandwalesmidyear2001to2019/",
  "deathsbylsoamidyear01to19.zip")
url_lsoa11 <- paste0("https://opendata.arcgis.com/api/v3/datasets/",
  "02e8d336d6804fbeabe6c972e5a27b16_0/downloads/data?format=geojson",
  "&spatialRefId=4326")
url_lsoa01 <- paste0("https://opendata.arcgis.com/api/v3/datasets/",
  "98b573a6f3ea483e97f7e08771624316_0/downloads/data?format=geojson",
  "&spatialRefId=4326")
url_lookup <- paste0("https://services1.arcgis.com/ESMARspQHYMw9BZ9/ArcGIS/",
  "rest/services/LSOA01_LSOA11_LAD11_EW_LU_ddfe1cd1c2784c9b991cded95bc915a9/",
  "FeatureServer/0/query")
url_worldpop <- "https://data.worldpop.org/GIS/AgeSex_structures/Global_2000_2020"
```

Statistical agencies revise published tables (Section 9.2), and portal URLs
change. We therefore **freeze** every processed input the first time it is
built: `freeze()` saves the object as a date-stamped `.rds` file and, on later
runs, loads the most recent saved copy instead of downloading again. To
refresh the data, delete the `.rds` files. The date stamp records when the
data were extracted, which belongs in any write-up.

```{r freeze-helper}
source(file.path("R", "download_helpers.R"))  # download_if_missing() etc.

freeze <- function(name, expr) {
  saved <- sort(list.files(data_dir, paste0("^", name, "_[0-9-]+\\.rds$"),
                           full.names = TRUE), decreasing = TRUE)
  if (length(saved) > 0) {
    message("Loading frozen ", basename(saved[1]))
    out <- readRDS(saved[1])
  } else {
    out <- expr                              # evaluated only if not frozen
    file <- file.path(data_dir, paste0(name, "_", Sys.Date(), ".rds"))
    saveRDS(if (inherits(out, "SpatRaster")) terra::wrap(out) else out, file)
  }
  if (inherits(out, "PackedSpatRaster")) out <- terra::unwrap(out)
  out
}
```

```{r frozen-files, echo = FALSE}
frozen <- list.files(data_dir, "_[0-9-]+\\.rds$")
```

The inputs used for this document were frozen on
`r if (length(frozen)) paste(unique(sub(".*_([0-9-]+)\\.rds$", "\\1", frozen)), collapse = ", ") else "the date of this run"`.

## Deaths

The ONS workbook has one row per mid-year and LSOA, with a column per age
band. "Mid-year 2008" covers deaths from 1 July 2007 to 30 June 2008. We keep
the two bands that make up under-5 mortality, `<1` and `01-04`, and name them
explicitly rather than matching column names by pattern, so that the age
range is visible in the code.

```{r deaths}
deaths11 <- freeze("deaths_u5_lsoa11", {
  zip <- download_if_missing(url_deaths,
                             file.path(data_dir, "deathsbylsoamidyear01to19.zip"))
  xlsx  <- unzip(zip, exdir = data_dir)
  sheet <- "Deaths - Persons"
  probe <- readxl::read_excel(xlsx, sheet, col_names = FALSE, n_max = 30,
                              .name_repair = "minimal")
  header_row <- which(tolower(probe[[1]]) == "mid-year")
  raw <- readxl::read_excel(xlsx, sheet, skip = header_row - 1)
  names(raw)[1:4] <- c("year", "lad", "lad_name", "lsoa11cd")
  under5_bands <- c("<1", "01-04")
  stopifnot(all(under5_bands %in% names(raw)))
  # The year is printed only on the first row of each block: fill it down.
  raw$year <- as.integer(sub(".*(20[0-9]{2}).*", "\\1", raw$year))
  raw$year <- data.table::nafill(raw$year, type = "locf")
  out <- raw %>%
    filter(year %in% years, lad %in% gm_lads) %>%
    transmute(year, lad, lad_name, lsoa11cd,
              deaths = as.numeric(`<1`) + as.numeric(`01-04`))
  stopifnot(setequal(unique(out$year), years))  # never freeze an empty table
  out
})
deaths11 %>% group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(lsoas = n(), deaths = sum(deaths), .groups = "drop")
```

## Boundaries and lookup

```{r boundaries}
lookup <- freeze("lsoa01_lsoa11_lookup", {
  fetch_arcgis_attrs(url_lookup,
                     out_fields = c("LSOA01CD", "LSOA11CD", "LAD11CD", "CHGIND"))
}) %>% as.data.frame() %>% filter(LAD11CD %in% gm_lads)

read_lsoa <- function(url, file, code) {
  download_if_missing(url, file.path(data_dir, file))
  st_read(file.path(data_dir, file), quiet = TRUE) %>%
    filter(.data[[code]] %in% unique(lookup[[code]])) %>%
    select(all_of(code)) %>%
    st_transform(uk_grid) %>%
    st_make_valid()
}
lsoa11 <- freeze("lsoa11_gm", read_lsoa(url_lsoa11, "lsoa11_bgc_ew.geojson",
                                        "LSOA11CD"))
lsoa01 <- freeze("lsoa01_gm", read_lsoa(url_lsoa01, "lsoa01_bgc_ew.geojson",
                                        "LSOA01CD"))
c(lsoa01 = nrow(lsoa01), lsoa11 = nrow(lsoa11))
table(change = lookup$CHGIND)
```

`CHGIND` describes each 2001--2011 link: `U` unchanged, `S` a 2001 LSOA
split into several 2011 LSOAs, `M` several 2001 LSOAs merged into one, and
`X` a more complex redrawing. About 4% of Greater Manchester's LSOAs changed.

## Population

WorldPop provides 100 m rasters of population counts by sex and age band. We
sum the four under-5 layers (female and male, ages 0 and 1--4) for each year,
crop to the study area, and reproject to a 200 m grid on the British National
Grid. The reprojection uses `method = "sum"` so that the population totals are
preserved (Section 9.3).

```{r population}
outline  <- st_union(lsoa11)
template <- rast(ext(vect(st_buffer(outline, 2000))), resolution = 200,
                 crs = uk_grid)

pop_u5 <- freeze("worldpop_u5_gm_200m", {
  layers <- lapply(years, function(yr) {
    files <- sapply(c("f_0", "f_1", "m_0", "m_1"), function(sa) {
      file <- sprintf("worldpop_gbr_%s_%d.tif", sa, yr)
      url  <- sprintf("%s/%d/GBR/gbr_%s_%d.tif", url_worldpop, yr, sa, yr)
      download_if_missing(url, file.path(data_dir, file))
    })
    r <- rast(files)
    r <- crop(r, project(vect(st_buffer(outline, 5000)), crs(r)))
    r <- project(sum(r, na.rm = TRUE), template, method = "sum")
    mask(r, vect(outline))
  })
  out <- rast(layers)
  names(out) <- years
  out
})
round(global(pop_u5, "sum", na.rm = TRUE))
```

# Data preparation

DAST needs two named lists with one element per period:

* `poly_list`: an `sf` object of polygons with an ID column and a count
  column, in a projected CRS;
* `offset_list`: a `SpatRaster` of population counts on a fine grid, in the
  same CRS.

## Reconstructing the 2001 geography for 2008--09

ONS now distributes these deaths on 2011 LSOAs for *all* years: the 2008--09
counts have been re-coded to the newer geography. Data as they were reported
at the time, and as many practitioners will hold them, are on 2001 LSOAs. To
reproduce that situation, we aggregate the 2008--09 counts back to the 2001
geography.

For unchanged and split LSOAs this is exact, because the 2011 children of a
split 2001 LSOA add up to the 2001 parent. Where 2001 LSOAs were merged or
redrawn, the 2001 parts cannot be recovered from 2011-coded counts, so we
dissolve the affected 2001 polygons into a single unit. The result is the
finest 2001-based geography recoverable from the published counts. In graph
terms, each unit is a connected component of the 2001--2011 lookup.

```{r units-2001}
# Label propagation over lookup links: every LSOA in a connected component
# of 2001 <-> 2011 links ends up with the component's smallest label.
a <- paste0("01:", lookup$LSOA01CD)
b <- paste0("11:", lookup$LSOA11CD)
label <- setNames(seq_along(unique(c(a, b))), unique(c(a, b)))
repeat {
  m   <- pmin(label[a], label[b])
  low <- tapply(c(m, m), c(a, b), min)
  new <- label
  new[names(low)] <- pmin(label[names(low)], low)
  if (all(new == label)) break
  label <- new
}
lookup$component <- label[a]
lookup <- lookup %>%
  group_by(component) %>%
  mutate(unit_id = if (n_distinct(LSOA01CD) == 1) LSOA01CD
                   else paste0(min(LSOA01CD), "+", n_distinct(LSOA01CD) - 1),
         change  = case_when(any(CHGIND %in% c("M", "X")) ~ "merged/redrawn",
                             any(CHGIND == "S") ~ "split",
                             TRUE ~ "unchanged")) %>%
  ungroup()

units01 <- lsoa01 %>%
  left_join(distinct(lookup, LSOA01CD, unit_id), by = "LSOA01CD") %>%
  group_by(unit_id) %>%
  summarise(do_union = TRUE, .groups = "drop")

lsoa11_to_unit <- distinct(lookup, LSOA11CD, unit_id)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(lsoa11_to_unit$LSOA11CD))  # each 2011 LSOA in 1 unit
nrow(units01)
```

## One `sf` object per period

```{r poly-list}
poly_list <- lapply(setNames(years, years), function(yr) {
  d <- filter(deaths11, year == yr)
  if (yr <= 2009) {               # 2001 geography
    counts <- d %>%
      inner_join(lsoa11_to_unit, by = c("lsoa11cd" = "LSOA11CD")) %>%
      group_by(AREA_ID = unit_id) %>%
      summarise(deaths = sum(deaths), .groups = "drop")
    units01 %>% rename(AREA_ID = unit_id) %>%
      left_join(counts, by = "AREA_ID")
  } else {                        # 2011 geography
    lsoa11 %>% rename(AREA_ID = LSOA11CD) %>%
      left_join(select(d, AREA_ID = lsoa11cd, deaths), by = "AREA_ID")
  }
})

# Offsets: one layer per period, named to match poly_list.
offset_list <- lapply(setNames(names(pop_u5), names(pop_u5)),
                      function(nm) pop_u5[[nm]])
```

Note the use of `left_join` with **no** `replace_na(deaths, 0)`: a polygon
without a matched count should stop the analysis, not quietly become a zero
(Section 9.1).

# Pre-fit checks

These checks are cheap, and each one targets a failure we actually
encountered. Run them before every fit, and in particular on any code
generated by an AI assistant.

```{r checks}
for (p in names(poly_list)) {
  x <- poly_list[[p]]
  d <- filter(deaths11, year == as.integer(p))
  # 1. every polygon has a count (no NA, no silent zero-fill)
  stopifnot(!anyNA(x$deaths))
  # 2. no count was lost when matching codes to polygons
  stopifnot(sum(x$deaths) == sum(d$deaths))
  # 3. polygon IDs are unique within the period
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(x$AREA_ID))
  # 4. polygons and offsets share a CRS
  stopifnot(st_crs(x) == st_crs(crs(offset_list[[p]])))
}
# 5. periods line up between the two lists
stopifnot(identical(names(poly_list), names(offset_list)))

# 6. every polygon has population in the offset
pop_in_poly <- sapply(names(poly_list), function(p)
  min(extract(offset_list[[p]], vect(poly_list[[p]]), fun = sum,
              na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)[[1]]))
stopifnot(all(pop_in_poly > 0))
```


## The boundary change

```{r boundary-plot-fn}
export_png <- function(file, expr, width = 5, height = 4.4) {
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) return(invisible())
  dir.create(dirname(file), showWarnings = FALSE)
  png(file, width = width, height = height, units = "in", res = 300)
  expr
  invisible(dev.off())
}

centre <- ext(383900 - 3500, 383900 + 3500, 398200 - 3000, 398200 + 3000)

plot_boundaries <- function() {
  bg <- openmap(vect(centre, crs = uk_grid), zoom = 13)
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  map.new(centre)
  plot(bg, add = TRUE)
  plot(crop(vect(lsoa11), centre), border = "#D55E00", lwd = 1.3, add = TRUE)
  plot(crop(vect(units01), centre), border = "black", lwd = 1.8, add = TRUE)
  legend("bottomright", lwd = c(1.8, 1.3), col = c("black", "#D55E00"),
         bg = "white", cex = 0.8, inset = 0.02,
         legend = c("2008-09 (2001 LSOAs)", "2010-12 (2011 LSOAs)"))
}
```

```{r boundary-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = "LSOA boundaries in Manchester city centre before and after the 2011 revision. Background map data © OpenStreetMap contributors."}
plot_boundaries()
export_png("output/manchester_boundaries.png", plot_boundaries(),
           width = 6, height = 5.2)
```

The figure shows the city centre, where the changes are concentrated:
population growth during the 2000s led ONS to split 2001 LSOAs that had grown
too large. Elsewhere in Greater Manchester the changes are scattered, and the
two geographies mostly coincide.

# Model specification

## Mesh

The random field $u(s)$ is represented on a triangular mesh (the SPDE
approach). `prepare_data_mmap()` builds the mesh from `mesh_args`, which are
passed to `fmesher`:

* `max.edge = c(inner, outer)`: the largest triangle edge inside the study
  area and in the extension around it. The inner value should be well below
  the spatial range you expect to resolve.
* `cutoff`: points closer than this are merged, which stops dense polygon
  vertices from producing tiny triangles.
* `offset = c(inner, outer)`: the width of the extension around the study
  area, which keeps boundary effects away from the data.
* `resolution`: the size of the grid on which the mesh is evaluated for
  prediction.

We scale these by the diagonal of the study area, as in the
Belgium--Netherlands example.

```{r prepare-data}
bb  <- st_bbox(poly_list[[1]])
diagonal <- sqrt((bb$xmax - bb$xmin)^2 + (bb$ymax - bb$ymin)^2)
maxedge  <- diagonal / 16

dis_data <- prepare_data_mmap(
  polygon_shapefile_list   = poly_list,
  aggregation_rasters_list = offset_list,
  response_var = "deaths",
  id_var       = "AREA_ID",
  na_action    = TRUE,
  mesh_args = list(max.edge = c(maxedge / 5, maxedge),
                   cutoff   = 0.2 * maxedge,
                   offset   = c(diagonal / 16, diagonal / 4),
                   resolution = 250)
)
c(diagonal_km = round(unname(diagonal) / 1000), mesh_nodes = dis_data$mesh$n)
```

```{r mesh, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Mesh vertices over the 2010 LSOAs."}
plot(vect(poly_list[["2010"]]), border = "grey60", lwd = 0.3)
points(dis_data$mesh$loc[, 1:2], pch = 15, cex = 0.25)
```

## Priors

All variance and range parameters have penalised-complexity (PC) priors.
Each prior is set by a statement about an implausible value rather than by
choosing a density directly:

* **range** $\rho$: $\Pr(\rho < \rho_0) = p_\rho$, i.e. how likely a range
  shorter than $\rho_0$ metres is;
* **spatial SD** $\sigma$: $\Pr(\sigma > \sigma_0) = p_\sigma$;
* **overdispersion** $\tau$: $\Pr(\tau > \tau_0) = p_\tau$. $\tau$ is the
  coefficient of variation of the gamma mixing distribution, so
  $\text{Var}(Y) = \mu + \tau^2\mu^2$, and $\tau = 0$ is the Poisson model.

`get_priors()` returns the defaults computed from the data. We override three
of them.

```{r priors}
priors <- get_priors(dis_data)
defaults <- priors
priors$prior_rho_min           <- 2500  # Pr(range < 2.5 km) = 0.5
priors$prior_rho_prob          <- 0.5
priors$prior_iideffect_sd_max  <- 0.1   # Pr(tau > 0.1) = 0.5
priors$prior_iideffect_sd_prob <- 0.5
priors$prior_sigma_max         <- 1     # Pr(sigma > 1) = 0.1

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  parameter = names(priors),
  default   = signif(unlist(defaults), 3),
  used      = signif(unlist(priors), 3)
), row.names = FALSE)
```

The default range bound is a third of the study-area diagonal, which suits a
smooth, regional surface. Here we want to resolve variation between
neighbourhoods of a city, so we put half the prior mass on ranges shorter
than 2.5 km. The default overdispersion prior, $\Pr(\tau > 0.1) = 0.01$, is
strongly anchored at Poisson. We relax it to $\Pr(\tau > 0.1) = 0.5$ so that
the data can show overdispersion if it is there. In either case the prior
shrinks towards Poisson, so no separate Poisson-versus-negative-binomial test
is needed: if the posterior for $\tau$ concentrates near zero, the fit is
effectively Poisson (Section 7.3). The default bound on the spatial SD allows
very large variation in risk. A spatial SD of 1 already lets the relative risk
vary from about 0.14 to 7 ($\pm 2$ SD), so we use $\Pr(\sigma > 1) = 0.1$, as
in the Belgium--Netherlands example.

## Likelihood and intercepts

`family = "negbinomial"` uses the gamma-mixed (negative binomial) likelihood
described in the paper. `family = "poisson"` with `iid = TRUE` gives the
lognormal alternative instead. `time_varying_betas = TRUE` gives each year
its own intercept $\beta_i$, which absorbs year-to-year changes in the overall
rate. The shared field $u(s)$ is then a relative-risk surface common to all
five years.

# Fitting

```{r fit}
fit_time <- system.time(
  fit <- disag_model_mmap(
    data   = dis_data,
    family = "negbinomial",
    link   = "log",
    iid    = TRUE,
    priors = priors,
    engine = "AGHQ",
    engine.args = list(aghq_k = 2,
                       optimizer = "nlminb"),  # see Section 9.5
    time_varying_betas = TRUE
  )
)
round(fit_time[["elapsed"]] / 60, 1)   # minutes
```

`engine = "AGHQ"` integrates over the hyperparameters and fixed effects,
$\theta = (\beta_{2008}, \ldots, \beta_{2012}, \log\tau, \log\sigma,
\log\rho)$, with adaptive Gauss--Hermite quadrature. It uses `aghq_k`
points per dimension, so $k^8$ points here, and integrates the latent field
with a Laplace approximation at each point. `aghq_k = 1` is the Laplace
approximation, which needs a single optimisation and is the fastest.
`aghq_k = 2` (256 points) captures skewness in the posterior at a
considerable cost. With `time_varying_betas = FALSE` there would be a single
intercept, $\theta$ would have four dimensions, and `aghq_k = 2` would need
16 points. Develop with `aghq_k = 1`, and use `aghq_k = 2` for the final run. We use the
`nlminb` optimiser for the outer optimisation because the default (BFGS)
failed on these data (Section 9.5).
On a desktop computer (one core in use) this fit took
`r round(fit_time[["elapsed"]] / 60)` minutes.

# Outputs

## Parameter summary

`summary(fit)` prints the full AGHQ summary, including the covariance matrix
used for quadrature. Here we extract the parameter table, then put it on
interpretable scales: the intercepts become baseline death rates per 1,000
children per year, and the range is given in kilometres.

```{r summary}
invisible(capture.output(
  s <- summary(fit$aghq_model, max_print = 0)$summarytable
))
rownames(s) <- c(paste0("intercept_", years), "log_tau", "log_sigma",
                 "log_rho")
round(s, 3)

natural <- exp(s[, c("2.5%", "median", "97.5%")])
natural[1:5, ] <- 1000 * natural[1:5, ]          # deaths per 1,000 per year
natural["log_rho", ] <- natural["log_rho", ] / 1000   # metres to km
rownames(natural) <- c(paste0("rate_", years), "tau", "sigma", "range_km")
round(natural, 2)
```

The baseline rate falls over the five years. The baseline is the rate where
$u(s) = 0$, so it is somewhat lower than the crude rate (deaths divided by
population), which is pulled up by the high-risk areas.

## Relative-risk and exceedance maps

We draw 500 samples from the posterior of the latent field and project them
onto the prediction grid. For each grid cell we compute the posterior median
of $\exp\{u(s)\}$, the relative risk compared with the year-specific
baseline, and the exceedance probability $\Pr\{u(s) > 0 \mid y\}$, the
probability that risk at $s$ is above that baseline.

```{r posterior-samples}
set.seed(2026)
samples <- aghq::sample_marginal(fit$aghq_model, M = 500)
pm <- DAST:::get_predict_matrices(       # internal helper
  data = fit$data,
  expected_cov_names = fit$model_setup$coef_meta$cov_names,
  time_varying_betas = TRUE
)
field <- pm$A %*% samples$samps          # cells x samples, log scale
surface <- rast(
  data.frame(pm$coords,
             rr  = exp(apply(field, 1, median)),
             exc = apply(field, 1, function(z) mean(z > 0))),
  crs = uk_grid
)
surface <- mask(surface, vect(outline))
```

```{r result-plot-fn}
lad_outline <- lsoa11 %>%
  left_join(distinct(lookup, LSOA11CD, LAD11CD), by = "LSOA11CD") %>%
  group_by(LAD11CD) %>% summarise(do_union = TRUE, .groups = "drop") %>%
  vect()
rr_col  <- colourScale(surface[["rr"]], breaks = 9, style = "equal",
                       transform = "log", col = "Spectral", rev = TRUE,
                       dec = 2)
exc_col <- colourScale(breaks = c(0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 1),
                       style = "fixed", col = "RdYlGn", rev = TRUE)

# One map per figure: terra's add = TRUE does not mix with multi-panel
# layouts, so each map gets its own device.
plot_layer <- function(layer, col, title) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  map.new(surface)
  plot(surface[[layer]], col = col$col, breaks = col$breaks,
       legend = FALSE, add = TRUE)
  plot(lad_outline, border = "grey20", lwd = 0.6, add = TRUE)
  legendBreaks("bottomleft", col, bty = "n", title = title, cex = 0.8)
}
```

```{r result-maps, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4.4, out.width = "49%", fig.show = "hold", fig.cap = "Under-5 mortality in Greater Manchester, 2008--2012. Left: posterior median relative risk. Right: posterior probability that relative risk exceeds 1. Lines are borough boundaries."}
plot_layer("rr", rr_col, "RR")
plot_layer("exc", exc_col, "Pr(RR>1)")
export_png("output/manchester_rr.png", plot_layer("rr", rr_col, "RR"))
export_png("output/manchester_exc.png",
           plot_layer("exc", exc_col, "Pr(RR>1)"))
```

## Prior and posterior distributions

Comparing prior and posterior shows how much the data inform each
hyperparameter. A posterior that looks like the prior means the data had
little to say, and the prior is driving the result.

```{r prior-posterior, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "Priors (dashed) and approximate posteriors (solid) for the hyperparameters."}
# Gaussian approximation on the log scale at the posterior mode, transformed
# to the natural scale (as in the Belgium--Netherlands example).
mode <- fit$aghq_model$optresults$mode
covm <- solve(fit$aghq_model$optresults$hessian)
pr   <- fit$obj$env$data
prior_dens <- list(
  log_rho = function(x) {
    lam <- -log(pr$prior_rho_prob) * pr$prior_rho_min
    lam / x^2 * exp(-lam / x)
  },
  log_sigma = function(x)
    dexp(x, -log(pr$prior_sigma_prob) / pr$prior_sigma_max),
  iideffect_log_tau = function(x)
    dexp(x, -log(pr$prior_iideffect_sd_prob) / pr$prior_iideffect_sd_max)
)
labels <- c(log_rho = "range (km)", log_sigma = "spatial SD",
            iideffect_log_tau = "NB overdispersion tau")
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
for (nm in names(prior_dens)) {
  i <- which(names(mode) == nm)
  z <- seq(mode[i] - 4 * sqrt(covm[i, i]), mode[i] + 4 * sqrt(covm[i, i]),
           length.out = 400)
  x <- exp(z)
  post  <- dnorm(z, mode[i], sqrt(covm[i, i])) / x   # Jacobian of exp()
  prior <- prior_dens[[nm]](x)
  scale <- if (nm == "log_rho") 1000 else 1
  matplot(x / scale, cbind(prior, post) * scale, type = "l", lty = c(2, 1),
          col = "black", xlab = labels[nm], ylab = "density", bty = "l")
}
```

```{r post-summaries, echo = FALSE}
post_rho_km <- round(exp(mode[["log_rho"]]) / 1000, 1)
post_tau    <- round(exp(mode[["iideffect_log_tau"]]), 2)
```

All three posteriors are much narrower than their priors, so the data are
informative about these parameters. The posterior mode of the range is about
`r post_rho_km` km, which is short compared with the conurbation and
consistent with variation between neighbourhoods. The posterior for $\tau$
is centred near `r post_tau`, well away from zero. The counts are therefore
clearly overdispersed compared with Poisson, and the negative binomial
likelihood matters here. Had the posterior for $\tau$ piled up at zero, the
fit would have been effectively Poisson.

# Interpretation

```{r interp-numbers, echo = FALSE}
v_rr  <- values(surface[["rr"]], na.rm = TRUE)
v_exc <- values(surface[["exc"]], na.rm = TRUE)
pct <- function(x) {
  v <- 100 * mean(x)
  if (v < 1) "less than 1%" else paste0(round(v), "%")
}
```

The posterior median relative risk ranges from
`r round(min(v_rr), 2)` to `r round(max(v_rr), 2)` across the conurbation,
with the central half of grid cells between
`r round(quantile(v_rr, 0.25), 2)` and `r round(quantile(v_rr, 0.75), 2)`.
On its own, the median map invites over-reading: any smooth surface fitted to
noisy counts will have highs and lows.

The exceedance map shows which of those highs and lows the data support. Only
`r pct(v_exc > 0.95)` of the area has $\Pr(\text{RR} > 1) > 0.95$, and
`r pct(v_exc < 0.05)` has $\Pr(\text{RR} > 1) < 0.05$. Over the remaining
`r pct(v_exc >= 0.05 & v_exc <= 0.95)` the data do not distinguish risk from
the baseline. That is the expected result with about 220 deaths a year spread
over 1,650 areas, and it is the main reason to report
exceedance alongside the median. The asymmetry is also informative. A few
clusters of elevated risk are well supported, but almost nowhere is risk
confidently *below* the baseline: with so few deaths, a further reduction
from an already low rate is very hard to detect. The supported clusters can
be followed up, while the rest of the map should not be interpreted area by
area.

Two further cautions apply. First, without covariates the surface below LSOA
scale is a smoothed interpolation, not new information about where deaths
occur within an LSOA. Second, $u(s)$ is shared across years, so the maps
summarise 2008--2012 as a whole and cannot show change over time.

# Common issues and debugging

## LSOA vintages and lookups

*Symptom:* counts silently disappear, or the fitted surface has holes or
spurious lows in particular neighbourhoods.
*Cause:* joining counts coded to one LSOA vintage onto polygons of another.
Most codes are identical in 2001 and 2011, so a join "mostly works". The
LSOAs that changed fail to match, and `replace_na(0)` turns them into areas
with zero deaths.
*Fix:* join through the official lookup and check totals before and after
every join (check 2 in Section 4). For example, the join used in the
AI-generated version of this analysis loses the following under-5 deaths:

```{r naive-join-demo}
deaths11 %>%
  mutate(matched = lsoa11cd %in% lookup$LSOA01CD) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(deaths), lost = sum(deaths[!matched]),
            .groups = "drop")
```

## Agencies re-code old years to new boundaries

*Symptom:* the data contain no boundary change where you expect one, or a
newer download disagrees with an older one.
*Cause:* agencies re-publish historical counts on current geographies. ONS
supplies 2001--2019 deaths on 2011 LSOAs (Section 3.1). Eurostat has
republished Belgian NUTS-3 counts from 2017 onwards on NUTS 2021 codes, which
is why the Belgium--Netherlands example (`disagg_EU.Rmd`) uses NUTS 2016
boundaries for 2015--16, NUTS 2021 for 2017--22 and NUTS 2024 for 2023.
*Fix:* for each period, confirm which boundary vintage the codes belong to,
for example by checking which code set they match. Freeze the data with an
extraction date (Section 2), and record that date in the paper.

## Raster CRS and alignment

*Symptom:* offsets of zero or NA for some polygons, population totals that
change after reprojection, or an error from `prepare_data_mmap()` about
extents.
*Cause:* WorldPop rasters are in longitude/latitude while the polygons are in
metres. Reprojecting a count raster with bilinear interpolation does not
preserve totals.
*Fix:* reproject to the polygons' CRS with `method = "sum"` onto an explicit
template grid. Check that each polygon has positive population (check 6) and
compare totals before and after reprojection.

## s2 versus GEOS topology errors

*Symptom:* `Loop 0 is not valid: Edge ... crosses edge ...` or
`duplicate vertex` errors from `sf` when unioning or intersecting UK
boundaries.
*Cause:* since version 1.0, `sf` uses the spherical s2 engine for
longitude/latitude data, and s2 is stricter than GEOS about polygon validity.
*Fix:* `sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)` at the start, transform to a projected CRS
early, and apply `st_make_valid()` after reading.

## AGHQ fails with `eigen()`: "infinite or missing values in 'x'"

*Symptom:* `disag_model_mmap()` stops after a long run with this error,
raised from `mvQuad::rescale()` inside `aghq`.
*Cause:* the Hessian of the hyperparameter posterior at its mode is not
finite, so the quadrature grid cannot be built. The Hessian is computed by
finite differences of the TMB gradient, and each evaluation needs an inner
Laplace optimisation that can fail at some perturbed parameter values. This
can happen with the default BFGS outer optimiser.
*Fix:* switch the outer optimiser with
`engine.args = list(aghq_k = 2, optimizer = "nlminb")`, which converged
here. If that also fails, fit with `aghq_k = 1` to find the problem more
quickly. Then look for polygons with tiny populations or for priors that
allow implausible ranges, and consider fewer intercepts
(`time_varying_betas = FALSE`).

## Other checks worth running

* a map of the raw counts for each period, to catch polygons outside the
  study area or misplaced IDs;
* fit with `aghq_k = 1` first: if that fails, more quadrature points will not
  help.

# Applying the method to your own data

The minimal inputs are:

1. **Polygons**, one `sf` object per period, in a projected CRS (metres), each
   with a unique ID column and a non-negative integer count column. The
   periods can have different polygons. Polygons should cover the same
   overall study region.
2. **Offsets**, one single-layer `SpatRaster` per period, holding the
   population at risk (counts, not densities) on a grid finer than the
   polygons, in the same CRS.
3. Both lists named by period, with the names in the same order.
4. Optionally, **covariates**, one `SpatRaster` per period with the same
   layer names in every period (`covariate_rasters_list`).

```{r template, eval = FALSE}
library(DAST)
library(sf)
library(terra)
sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)

# 1. one sf per period: ID column + count column, projected CRS
poly_list <- list(
  "2015" = st_read("areas_2015.gpkg") |> st_transform(3035),
  "2016" = st_read("areas_2016.gpkg") |> st_transform(3035)
)
# 2. one population raster per period, same CRS, names match poly_list
offset_list <- list(
  "2015" = project(rast("pop_2015.tif"), "EPSG:3035", method = "sum"),
  "2016" = project(rast("pop_2016.tif"), "EPSG:3035", method = "sum")
)
# 3. checks from Section 4: no NA counts, totals preserved, unique IDs,
#    same CRS, names match, positive population in every polygon

# 4. data object and mesh (scale mesh_args to your study area)
dis_data <- prepare_data_mmap(
  polygon_shapefile_list = poly_list, aggregation_rasters_list = offset_list,
  response_var = "count", id_var = "area_id", na_action = TRUE)

# 5. priors: start from the defaults and change only what you can justify
priors <- get_priors(dis_data)

# 6. fit; try aghq_k = 1 first
fit <- disag_model_mmap(dis_data, priors = priors, family = "negbinomial",
                        engine = "AGHQ",
                        engine.args = list(aghq_k = 1, optimizer = "nlminb"),
                        time_varying_betas = TRUE)
summary(fit)
```

# Using an AI assistant

The first version of this analysis was generated by an AI coding assistant
(Codex), from a short prompt that pointed it at the Belgium--Netherlands
example. That code is kept unchanged in `final_manchester_2008_2012.Rmd`.

**What worked.** The assistant found the right data sources, wrote working
download code for them (reused here in `R/download_helpers.R`), and adapted
the model-fitting code from the example correctly. That code is short and
follows a fixed pattern.

**What needed human checking.** All the problems were in data assembly, and
none of them produced an error:

* *study area*: the code selected all ten Greater Manchester boroughs when
  "Manchester" was asked for;
* *age range*: it summed deaths at ages 0--19, while the population offset
  was under-5;
* *boundary vintage*: it assumed the 2008--09 counts were on 2001 LSOAs. They
  are on 2011 LSOAs, so changed areas failed to match and were set to zero
  (the table in Section 9.1).

Our own debugging fixed the problems that caused errors. The
boundary error is caught by checks 1 and 2 in Section 4. The study area and
age range are not errors that a check of internal consistency can catch:
they are found by reading the code against the question and by comparing
the totals with a published figure.

**Recommendations.** Give the assistant a working example to adapt, as we
did. This document is designed to be a very clear and strong example.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
